parts.problem_md: Calculate the molar mass of oxygen gas, O<sub>2</sub> and give the associated unit.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the molar mass of oxygen gas:

- The atomic mass of oxygen is 16
- Therefore, one mole of oxygen atoms = 16 g
- Therefore, one mole of oxygen gas, O<sub>2</sub> = 2 × 16 = 32 g
- So the molar mass, $M_{r}$ = 32 **[1 mark]**
- Unit = g mol<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

Calculate the molar mass of oxygen gas, O~2~ and give the associated unit.
To calculate the molar mass of oxygen gas: The atomic mass of oxygen is 16. Therefore, one mole of oxygen atoms = 16 g. Therefore, one mole of oxygen gas, O~2~ = 2 × 16 = 32 g. So the molar mass, Mr = 32. Unit = g mol^−1.

Calculate the number of moles in 0.5 kg of oxygen gas.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the number of moles in 0.5 kg of O<sub>2</sub> gas:

List the known values:

- Molar mass of O<sub>2</sub>, $M_{r}$ = 32 g mol<sup>−1</sup> (from part (c))
- Mass of O<sub>2</sub> = 0.5 kg = 500 g

Recall the molar mass equation:

- $n=\frac{m}{M_{r}}$
- $n=\frac{500}{32}$ **[1 mark]**
- $n=15.625\mathrm{mol}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *When dealing with molar mass (units grams per mole) it is easier to keep the units in grams.*

parts.problem_md: Determine the number of atoms in 4.0 g of Nitrogen-14.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Atomic mass of nitrogen-14 = mass of 1 mole of nitrogen-14 = 14 g
- Mass of nitrogen sample, *m *= 4.0 g
- Avogadro's constant, *N*<sub>*A*</sub> = 6.02 × 10<sup>23 </sup>mol<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the number of moles in 4.0 g:

- $n=\frac{\mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{sample}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{mass}}$** [1 mark]**
- $n=\frac{4}{14}=0.2857$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the number of atoms, *N*:

- *N *= *n *× *N*<sub>*A*</sub> **[1 mark]**
- *N* = 0.2857 × (6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup>)
- *N *= 1.72 × 10<sup>23</sup> = 1.7 × 10<sup>23</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *When doing molar calculations it is important to leave the unrounded **n** number in your calculator to use in the **N** calculation. Because you are multiplying by such a large number (6.02 × 10*<sup>*23*</sup>*) any rounding errors are greatly magnified. If you use the unrounded value for n, then **N **= 1.72 × 10*<sup>*23*</sup>* but if you use **n** = 0.29 then **N **= 1.746 × 10*<sup>*23*</sup>* = 1.75 × 10*<sup>*23 *</sup>*which may lose you the mark.*

equations.alt: n space equals space fraction numerator mass space of space sample over denominator molar space mass end fraction space
n space equals space 4 over 14 space equals space 0.2857

parts.problem_md: Explain the difference in the nuclear composition of nitrogen-14 and nitrogen-15.
parts.solution_md:
An isotope is:

- An atom of the same element that has the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons in the nucleus; **[1 mark]**

Nitrogen-14 is:

- An isotope of nitrogen that has 14 nucleons; **[1 mark]**
- 7 protons and 7 neutrons; **[1 mark]**

Nitrogen-15 is:

- An isotope of nitrogen that has 15 nucleons; **[1 mark]**
- 7 protons and 8 neutrons; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Atomic mass of nitrogen-14 = mass of 1 mole of nitrogen-14 = 14 g
Nitrogen-14 has 14 nucleons (7 protons and 7 neutrons); Nitrogen-15 has 15 nucleons (7 protons and 8 neutrons).

State whether there are more atoms in 4 g of nitrogen-14 than in nitrogen-15. Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
The number of atoms in nitrogen-15 is:

- Less than the number of atoms in nitrogen-14; **[1 mark]**

This is because:

- The molar mass of nitrogen-15 is bigger than the molar mass of nitrogen-14 so the number of moles *n  *will be less; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
The following information on the isotopes of the elements in methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>) is available:

- Carbon-12
- Hydrogen-1
- Sulphur-32
- Oxygen-16

(i) Determine the ratio of the molar mass of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>).

[3]

(ii) State the number of moles of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) required to equal the same mass of sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>).

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i) Determine the molar mass of methane, CH<sub>4</sub>:

- Molar mass of carbon-12 = 12 g
- Molar mass of hydrogen-1 = 1 g
- Molar mass of CH<sub>4 </sub>= 12 + (4 × 1) = 16 g **[1 mark]**

Determine the molar mass of sulphur dioxide, SO<sub>2</sub>:

- Molar mass of sulphur-32 = 32 g
- Molar mass of oxygen-16 = 16 g
- Molar mass of SO<sub>2 </sub>= 32 + (16 × 2) = 32 + 32 = 64 g **[1 mark]**

Obtain a ratio for the molar mass of methane and sulphur dioxide:

- $\frac{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{mass} \mathrm{methane}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{mass} \mathrm{sulphur} \mathrm{dioxide}}=\frac{16}{64}=0.25$** [1 mark]**

(ii) State the number of moles of methane required to equal the same mass of sulphur dioxide:

- 4 moles of methane are required;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

equations.alt: fraction numerator molar space mass space methane over denominator molar space mass space sulphur space dioxide end fraction space equals space 16 over 64 space equals space 0.25

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The following information on the isotopes of the elements in methane (CH~4~) and sulphur dioxide (SO~2~) is available:
- Carbon-12
- Hydrogen-1
- Sulphur-32
- Oxygen-16

Methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>) are mixed together in equal parts to form a gas of mass 880 g.

Determine the number of moles of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>) contained within the gas.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Molar mass SO<sub>2</sub> = 64 g
- Molar mass CH<sub>4</sub> = 16 g
- Mass of mixed gas, *m  *= 880 g

Determine the combined molar mass of SO<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>4</sub>:

- Combined molar mass = 64 + 16 = 80 g **[1 mark]**

Calculate the number of moles of SO<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>4</sub>:

- Number of moles = $\frac{880}{80}=11$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the number of moles of CH<sub>4</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub>:

- Gases are mixed in equal parts, so there are <u>11 moles</u> of <u>both</u> CH<sub>4</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Don't let part (a) confuse you. The gases have been combined as one molecule of SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* with one molecule of CH*<sub>*4*</sub>*.*

equations.alt: 880 over 80 space equals space 11

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The following information on the isotopes of the elements in methane (CH~4~) and sulphur dioxide (SO~2~) is available: Carbon-12, Hydrogen-1, Sulphur-32, Oxygen-16. Molar mass of CH4 = 12 + (4 × 1) = 16 g. Molar mass of SO2 = 32 + (16 × 2) = 64 g.

In a new mix of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>) of mass 896 g. The two gases have been mixed in the ratio 4:1 methane to sulphur dioxide.

Determine the number of moles of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>) contained within the gas.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Molar mass SO<sub>2</sub> = 64 g (From part (a))
- Molar mass CH<sub>4</sub> = 16 g (From part (a))
- Mass of mixed gas, *m *= 896 g

Determine the mass of each substance:

- Ratio is CH<sub>4 </sub>: SO<sub>2 </sub>, 4:1
- Molar mass fits this ratio (4 × 16 g = 64 g): (1 × 64 g) therefore, in terms of mass the gases are equally split

  - $\frac{896}{2}=448$ g SO<sub>2</sub> and 448 g CH<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**

Determine the number of moles of each substance:

- Moles of CH<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{448}{16}=28$ **[1 mark]**
- Moles of SO<sub>2</sub> = $\frac{448}{64}=7$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Hopefully, you recognised that the ratio given is the same as the ratio already calculated in part (a). So no additional sums are needed here.  There are several ways to complete this question but this method follows the most logical steps for 3 marks. *

Determine the mass of carbon in 600 g of glucose.
parts.solution_md:
To determine the mass of carbon in 600 g of glucose:

List the known quantities:

- Atomic mass of carbon = 12
- Number of glucose molecules, *N* = 2.01 ×10<sup>24</sup> (from part (c))
- Unified atomic mass unit, 1 u = 1.66×10<sup>−27</sup> kg (from the data page)

Determine the number of carbon atoms in 600 g of glucose:

- There are 6 carbon atoms per C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> molecule
- Therefore, there are 6*N* carbon atoms in 600 g of glucose

  - Number of C atoms = $6\times2.01\times10^{24}$** [1 mark]**
  - Number of C atoms = $1.206\times10^{25}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the total mass of carbon atoms:

- Mass of 1 carbon atom = 12 u = $12\times1.66\times10^{-27}=1.992\times10^{-26}\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**
- Total mass of carbon atoms = mass of 1 carbon atom × number of carbon atoms

  - Total mass of carbon atoms = `open parentheses 1.992 cross times 10 to the power of negative 26 end exponent close parentheses space cross times space open parentheses 1.206 cross times 10 to the power of 25 close parentheses` **[1 mark]**
  - Total mass of carbon atoms = $0.240\mathrm{kg}$  **OR** 240 g** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**
